title: Are three sixths, four eighths and five tenths equivalent?
description: Each fraction is compared with one half: the top number is half of the bottom number in all three. On the fraction wall the three lengths end at the same place, and multiplying one half by three, four and five checks it.
teaching_notes: One idea: a fraction whose top number is half of its bottom number is equal to one half. Watch for students who think different numbers must give different lengths.

source: Figure it Out Q1 (section 7.6, first block)
video_script.why: A learner decides whether three fractions are equivalent by comparing each with one half on the fraction wall.
video_script.substitution: none: the book's own fraction wall with rows of sixths, eighths and tenths
video_script.anchor: the fraction wall of the book: one whole and rows of equal pieces
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, all three lengths are equal, because each one equals one half

final_answer.value: Yes. On the fraction wall all three lengths are equal (each equals 1/2).
final_answer.spoken: yes, all three lengths are equal and each equals one half

video_script.fraction_reading: three sixths, four eighths, five tenths, one half
maths_rules: all three end at the middle of the whole on the fraction wall
check: 1/2 with top and bottom times 3 gives 3/6, times 4 gives 4/8, times 5 gives 5/10
video_script.design: One idea: compare each fraction with one half. The wall stays on screen with a guide line at the middle of the whole.
